blocks.text: Most human diseases result from microbial infections: invasions of the body by viruses, pathogenic bacteria, fungi or protists. To defend against infections and against cancers, vertebrates have the immune system, which continually checks the bloodstream for foreign cells and molecules. When it detects an infection it attacks and destroys the invaders; that is why diseases that weaken it, such as AIDS, are so dangerous.

blocks.title: Tidbit: a defended city
blocks.text: The body is defended like a city against invasion: walls make entry difficult, roaming police check strangers, and security guards challenge anyone without proper identification and call the police. The body likewise has several lines of defence.

blocks.alt: A vertical flowchart. Invasive microbe, then FIRST LINE OF DEFENCE, non-specific: skin, digestive tract, respiratory tract. 'If first line of defence is penetrated, the body responds with' SECOND LINE OF DEFENCE, non-specific: killer cells of blood, antimicrobial proteins, inflammation, fever. 'If second line of defence is penetrated, the body responds with' THIRD LINE OF DEFENCE, specific: cell-mediated immunity, antibody-mediated immunity.
blocks.caption: Figure 21.1: Lines of defence against infection (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 21.1).

blocks.text: The first line of defence consists of the skin, the digestive tract and the respiratory tract.
